devops-docker.tldr:
• Multi-stage builds with Spring Boot layers make rebuilds and pushes small.
  • Run as non-root on a JRE or distroless base; log to stdout.
  • Buildpacks and Jib build good images without a Dockerfile.
  • Tag immutably, deploy by digest, scan and sign images.
devops-docker.body:
Goals: small images, fast rebuilds (cache-friendly layers), no build tools or source in the runtime image, non-root user, reproducible tags.

Multi-stage Dockerfile with Spring Boot layered jars (Spring Boot 3.3+ tools jar mode):

Dockerfile
# ---- build stage: compile and package ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY .mvn .mvn
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN ./mvnw -B -q dependency:go-offline          # cached until pom.xml changes
COPY src src
RUN ./mvnw -B -q package -DskipTests

# ---- extract stage: split the fat jar into layers ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS extract
WORKDIR /extract
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination extracted

# ---- runtime stage: JRE only, non-root ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 --no-create-home spring
WORKDIR /app
# least-changing layers first, so a code change only rebuilds/pushes the small 'application' layer
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /extract/extracted/application/ ./
USER 10001
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

Why layers matter: your dependencies (~80 MB) rarely change, your own classes (~1 MB) change every build. With one fat-jar layer, every deploy pushes and pulls the whole thing; with layers, only the last small layer moves. (On Spring Boot 2.x / 3.0–3.2 the equivalent is -Djarmode=layertools ... extract.)

Text
# .dockerignore — keep the build context small and secrets out of images
target/
.git/
.idea/
*.iml
.env
**/*.log

Why layer order matters

Alternatives that need no Dockerfile

Tool Command Notes
Cloud Native Buildpacks ./mvnw spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=registry.example/order-service:1.4.2 layered, non-root, memory calculator built in; needs a Docker daemon
Jib ./mvnw compile jib:build -Dimage=registry.example/order-service:1.4.2 builds and pushes without Docker, reproducible layers

Base image choices

Image Size Trade-off
eclipse-temurin:21-jre (Ubuntu) ~200 MB shell and tools for debugging; more CVEs to patch
eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine smaller musl libc; occasionally surprises with native libraries
gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12 small no shell or package manager (smaller attack surface); debug with kubectl debug ephemeral containers
custom jlink runtime smallest only the JDK modules you use; more build complexity

Image hygiene

  • Tag images immutably (1.4.2, git SHA) and deploy by digest; never deploy latest.
  • Scan in CI (Trivy, Grype) and fail on critical CVEs with fixes available; rebuild regularly to pick up base-image patches.
  • Sign images (cosign) and verify at admission in the cluster.
  • Run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem (securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, mount /tmp as an emptyDir).
  • One process per container; logs to stdout/stderr, not files.

devops-jvm.tldr:
• The JVM reads cgroup limits; default max heap is only 25% of the limit — set MaxRAMPercentage.
  • CPU count comes from CPU limits; without limits, pin ActiveProcessorCount.
  • Small containers default to Serial GC: choose G1 or ZGC explicitly.
  • Speed startup with CDS/AOT caches, CRaC or native images.
devops-jvm.body:
Modern JVMs (JDK 10+, and 8u191+) are container-aware: they read the cgroup memory and CPU limits instead of the host's. Knowing how they derive their settings prevents most container problems.

Memory

Flag Default Advice
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage 25% of the container limit for the max heap 60–75% for typical services, leaving room for non-heap memory
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage 1.5625% set equal to max for latency-sensitive services to avoid heap growth pauses
-Xmx — avoid together with percentages; a fixed -Xmx silently breaks when someone changes the limit

Non-heap memory (Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, GC structures, direct buffers, native) typically needs 200–500 MB, so a 512 MB container with 75% heap is tight while a 2 GB container with 75% is comfortable. See Production Debugging → OOMKilled for the full breakdown.

CPU

  • The JVM sizes GC threads, the ForkJoin common pool and JIT compiler threads from availableProcessors(), which it derives from the CPU limit (CFS quota). Since JDK 19 it ignores CPU requests (shares).
  • No CPU limit → it sees every core on the node (say 64) and creates many GC and pool threads. Pin it with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=4 when you run without limits.
  • With fewer than 2 CPUs or less than ~1.8 GB of memory the JVM considers itself a client machine and picks Serial GC. Set -XX:+UseG1GC (or ZGC) explicitly.
Shell
# What did the JVM actually decide inside the container?
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MaxHeapSize|UseSerialGC|UseG1GC|ActiveProcessorCount"
jcmd 1 VM.info | grep -iE "container|cpus|memory limit"
jcmd 1 VM.flags

Faster startup (matters for autoscaling and rolling deploys)

Technique Gain Cost
Class Data Sharing (AppCDS); Spring Boot 3.3 has built-in support ~20–40% faster startup a training run at build time
JDK 24+ ahead-of-time class loading & linking cache (JEP 483) larger gains than CDS newer JDK
CRaC (checkpoint/restore; Spring Boot 3.2+) starts in milliseconds from a warmed snapshot Linux-only, snapshot management, secrets in snapshots
GraalVM native image (./mvnw -Pnative native:compile) ~100 ms startup, low memory long builds, reflection configuration, lower peak throughput for some workloads
Lazy initialization (spring.main.lazy-initialization=true) faster startup first requests slower, errors surface later
YAML
# Typical container env for a Spring Boot service
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: >-
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=70
      -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
      -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
      -Xlog:gc*:stdout:time,uptime,level,tags

devops-k8s.tldr:
• Deployments manage stateless pods through ReplicaSets; Services give stable names and load balancing.
  • ConfigMaps and Secrets inject config; PDBs protect availability during drains.
  • Spread replicas across zones; run non-root with read-only filesystems.
  • StatefulSets are for stateful systems that need identity and volumes.
devops-k8s.body:
Object Purpose
Pod one or more containers sharing network and volumes; the unit of scheduling; disposable
Deployment desired state for stateless pods (replicas, image, strategy); manages ReplicaSets for rollouts and rollbacks
Service stable name and virtual IP load-balancing to ready pods selected by labels (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer)
Ingress / Gateway API HTTP routing from outside the cluster (host/path rules, TLS)
ConfigMap / Secret configuration and sensitive values, injected as env vars or files
StatefulSet stable identities and per-pod volumes (Kafka, databases)
Job / CronJob run-to-completion and scheduled work
HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale replicas on metrics
PodDisruptionBudget limit voluntary disruptions (node drains)
ServiceAccount + RBAC pod identity and API permissions; cloud workload identity
NetworkPolicy which pods may talk to which (default-deny for zero trust)

A complete, production-shaped manifest

YAML
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
  labels: { app: order-service }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }       # never drop below desired capacity
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: order-service }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: order-service
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      topologySpreadConstraints:                                # spread replicas across zones
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry.example/order-service:1.4.2
          ports: [ { name: http, containerPort: 8080 } ]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: order-service-config }
            - secretRef: { name: order-service-secrets }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" }
            limits:   { memory: "1Gi" }
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 30                                # up to 150 s to start
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"] } }
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          volumeMounts: [ { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp } ]
      volumes: [ { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} } ]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  selector: { app: order-service }
  ports: [ { name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http } ]
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }

Other services reach it at http://order-service (same namespace) or http://order-service.shop.svc.cluster.local.

devops-probes.tldr:
• Startup for slow starts, readiness for traffic, liveness for restarts.
  • Never put shared dependencies in liveness checks.
  • A preStop sleep plus graceful shutdown prevents 502s during rollouts.
  • Fit shutdown phases inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

devops-resources.tldr:
• Requests schedule, limits enforce: CPU over limit throttles, memory over limit kills.
  • Set memory request = limit; be cautious with CPU limits for JVMs.
  • HPA uses utilization relative to requests; scale I/O-bound services on traffic or lag (KEDA).
  • Use VPA recommendations to right-size.
devops-resources.body:
Requests vs limits

Request Limit
Used for scheduling (the node must have this much unreserved) runtime enforcement
CPU over the value allowed if the node has spare CPU throttled (CFS quota per 100 ms period): the process waits
Memory over the value allowed if the node has spare memory (but evicted first under pressure) OOMKilled

QoS classes (decide eviction order under node pressure)

Class Condition Eviction priority
Guaranteed every container has requests = limits for both CPU and memory last
Burstable some requests or limits set, not Guaranteed middle
BestEffort nothing set first

Practical settings for JVM services

  • Memory: request = limit. Memory isn't compressible; overcommitting memory leads to OOMKills and evictions at the worst time. Size the limit from measured usage plus headroom, and the heap from the limit with MaxRAMPercentage.
  • CPU: set requests from measured usage; be careful with limits. CPU limits cause throttling even when the node is idle, and JVMs burst at startup (JIT compilation, class loading) and during GC. Common choices: no CPU limit (plus -XX:ActiveProcessorCount), or a limit well above the request. Watch container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total.
  • Startup takes far more CPU than steady state; slow starts under tight CPU limits make rolling updates and autoscaling sluggish.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

YAML
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: order-service }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 65 } }   # % of the CPU REQUEST
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300          # avoid flapping
      policies: [ { type: Percent, value: 20, periodSeconds: 60 } ]
  • CPU utilization is relative to requests: wrong requests mean wrong scaling.
  • For I/O-bound services, CPU is a poor signal; scale on request rate or latency (custom metrics through Prometheus Adapter) or on queue depth.
  • KEDA scales on external signals such as Kafka consumer lag, SQS queue length or cron windows (and can scale to zero):
YAML
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: order-indexer }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: order-indexer }
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 12                        # never more than the topic's partition count
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: order-indexer
        topic: orders
        lagThreshold: "1000"                 # target lag per replica
  • Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends (or applies) requests from observed usage: run it in recommendation mode to right-size.
  • Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter add nodes when pods can't be scheduled. Scaling pods is fast; adding nodes takes minutes, so keep some headroom.

devops-config.tldr:
• Env vars need restarts; mounted files update in place.
  • Trigger rolling updates on config change with a checksum annotation.
  • Kubernetes Secrets are only base64: encrypt etcd, restrict RBAC, sync from a secrets manager.
  • Validate config at startup.
devops-config.body:
ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, Secrets for sensitive values. Two ways to consume them:

Environment variables Mounted files
Spring binding relaxed binding: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL → spring.datasource.url spring.config.import=configtree:/etc/config/ or an application.yml file
Updates require a pod restart files update in place (~1 min), the app must re-read them
Visibility visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, crash dumps file permissions
YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: order-service-config }
data:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
  APP_PAYMENT_BASE_URL: https://pay.internal
  APP_PAYMENT_TIMEOUT: 2s
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: { name: order-service-secrets }
type: Opaque
stringData:                        # in real clusters this comes from a secrets manager, not from git
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: change-me
YAML
# Spring Boot reading a mounted directory of files (one file per key)
spring:
  config:
    import: "optional:configtree:/etc/secrets/"

Rolling out config changes safely: a ConfigMap change doesn't restart pods. Put a hash of the config into a pod annotation (Helm: checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}) so every config change triggers a normal rolling update, with health checks and easy rollback. Avoid live-reloading critical config in place without validation.

Secrets done properly

  • Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded: enable encryption at rest for etcd and lock down RBAC (get secrets is powerful).
  • Keep the source of truth in a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) and sync with External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver; or use Sealed Secrets / SOPS to store encrypted secrets in git for GitOps.
  • Prefer workload identity (IRSA on EKS, Workload Identity on GKE/AKS) so pods get short-lived cloud credentials without any stored keys.

Twelve-factor config: the same image runs in every environment; only config differs. Validate it at startup (@ConfigurationProperties + @Validated) so a bad value fails the rollout instead of the first request.

devops-deploy.tldr:
• Rolling updates are the default; blue/green and canaries reduce risk at a cost.
  • Argo Rollouts automates canary analysis on metrics.
  • Helm packages manifests with values; --atomic rolls back failed upgrades.
  • GitOps makes deploys pull requests and rollbacks reverts.
devops-deploy.body:
Deployment strategies on Kubernetes

Strategy How Rollback Needs
Rolling update (default) replace pods gradually (maxSurge, maxUnavailable) kubectl rollout undo backward-compatible versions running side by side
Blue/green full new ReplicaSet, switch the Service selector at once switch back double capacity during the switch
Canary send a small % of traffic to the new version, increase while metrics stay healthy shift traffic back traffic splitting (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, a mesh or Gateway API weights)
Feature flags deploy dark, enable per user/percentage flip the flag flag service (Unleash, LaunchDarkly, OpenFeature)

Canary with automated analysis (Argo Rollouts)

YAML
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis: { templates: [ { templateName: error-rate-below-1pct } ] }   # Prometheus query; auto-abort on failure
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
  template: { }            # same pod template as a Deployment (omitted here)

Helm: packaging manifests with values

Text
order-service/
  Chart.yaml               # name, version, appVersion
  values.yaml              # defaults
  values-prod.yaml         # environment overrides
  templates/
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    hpa.yaml
    configmap.yaml
    _helpers.tpl
YAML
# templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
Shell
helm lint ./order-service
helm template ./order-service -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
helm upgrade --install order-service ./order-service -n shop -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m
helm rollback order-service 7 -n shop

--atomic rolls the release back automatically if the upgrade doesn't become healthy in time.

GitOps (Argo CD / Flux): the desired state of every environment lives in git; an in-cluster controller continuously applies it and shows drift. Deploying becomes a pull request that bumps an image tag; rollback is a revert. Audit trail and review come for free.

devops-cicd.tldr:
• Stages: build/test → Testcontainers → static and dependency scans → image build/scan/sign → staging → canary.
  • Build once and promote the same image digest.
  • Keep pipelines fast with caching and parallel tests.
  • Rollback is one rehearsed command; migrations stay backward compatible.
devops-cicd.body:
Stages and what each one catches

Stage Tools Fails the build when
Build & unit tests Maven/Gradle, JUnit 5, Mockito tests fail, coverage gate missed
Integration tests Testcontainers (Postgres, Kafka, Redis), @SpringBootTest real infrastructure behaviour breaks
Static analysis SonarQube, SpotBugs, Checkstyle, Error Prone new bugs/code smells over thresholds
Dependency & secret scanning OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, Dependabot, gitleaks critical CVEs, leaked secrets
Image Jib/Buildpacks/Docker, Trivy, cosign critical CVEs in the image
Staging deploy Helm / Argo CD rollout not healthy
Verification smoke tests, Pact verification, k6/Gatling broken contract, latency regression
Production Argo Rollouts / Flagger canary error rate or latency worse than baseline

GitHub Actions example

YAML
name: ci
on:
  push: { branches: [ main ] }
  pull_request:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write, id-token: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: "21", cache: maven }
      - name: Build, unit and integration tests
        run: ./mvnw -B verify                       # Testcontainers works on GitHub-hosted runners (Docker available)
      - name: Dependency scan
        run: ./mvnw -B org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check -DfailBuildOnCVSS=9
      - name: Build and push image
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: ./mvnw -B compile jib:build -Dimage=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          -Djib.to.auth.username=${{ github.actor }} -Djib.to.auth.password=${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Scan image
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with: { image-ref: "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}", severity: CRITICAL, exit-code: "1" }

Principles: build once and promote the same artifact (image digest) through environments; keep pipelines fast (cache dependencies, run test slices in parallel); every merge to main is deployable; database migrations are backward compatible so app and schema can roll independently; rollback is one command and rehearsed.

devops-observability.tldr:
• Prometheus scrapes metrics, Loki stores logs, Tempo stores traces; Grafana ties them together.
  • Enable percentile histograms for accurate p99 across pods.
  • Alert on SLO error-budget burn rates over two windows.
  • Put trace ids in logs and use exemplars to jump from metrics to traces.
devops-observability.body:
The three signals and where they go

Instrumenting the service

YAML
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health, info, prometheus
  metrics:
    tags: { application: order-service }
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true        # histogram buckets -> accurate p95/p99 across pods
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability:4318/v1/traces
logging.structured.format.console: ecs   # Spring Boot 3.4+: JSON logs with traceId/spanId

Alternatively, attach the OpenTelemetry Java agent (-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar, configured with OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT) for zero-code instrumentation of HTTP, JDBC, Kafka and Redis clients.

Scraping with the Prometheus Operator

YAML
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata: { name: order-service, labels: { release: prometheus } }
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
  endpoints: [ { port: http, path: /actuator/prometheus, interval: 15s } ]

PromQL you'll actually use

Text
# Request rate per endpoint
sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order-service"}[5m]))

# Error ratio (5xx / all)
sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order-service", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order-service"}[5m]))

# p99 latency per endpoint (needs percentiles-histogram enabled)
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{application="order-service"}[5m])))

# JVM: heap used after GC trend, GC pause max, Hikari saturation, CPU throttling
jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"}
max_over_time(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_max[5m])
hikaricp_connections_pending
rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{container="app"}[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{container="app"}[5m])

Alert on symptoms, against SLOs. Define an SLO (e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed under 500 ms over 30 days) and alert on error-budget burn rate using two windows (the multi-window, multi-burn-rate approach from the Google SRE workbook): page when the budget burns ~14× faster than allowed over both the last hour and the last 5 minutes; open a ticket for slow burns. This catches real user impact while avoiding pages for brief blips. Keep cause-based alerts (disk 80% full, certificate expiring) as tickets, not pages.

Correlate: put traceId in every log line (Micrometer Tracing does it via MDC), enable exemplars so a latency spike on a Grafana panel links to an example trace, and link traces to logs in Grafana (Tempo → Loki by trace id).

devops-debugging.tldr:
• Start with get, describe, logs --previous and events.
  • Know the pod states: Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, Evicted.
  • Debug distroless pods with ephemeral containers (kubectl debug).
  • Unreachable service: readiness → selector/endpoints → ports → NetworkPolicy → ingress → DNS.
devops-debugging.body:
Everyday commands

Shell
kubectl get pods -n shop -o wide                      # status, restarts, node, IP
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n shop                    # events: scheduling, probes, OOMKilled, image pulls
kubectl logs <pod> -n shop -c app --since=15m         # current container logs
kubectl logs <pod> -n shop --previous                 # logs of the crashed previous container
kubectl logs -l app=order-service -n shop --tail=50 --prefix   # across all replicas
kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
kubectl top pod -n shop --containers                  # CPU/memory now (metrics-server)
kubectl exec -it <pod> -n shop -- sh                  # shell (if the image has one)
kubectl debug -it <pod> -n shop --image=eclipse-temurin:21-jdk --target=app   # ephemeral debug container, shares the process namespace
kubectl port-forward svc/order-service 8080:80 -n shop                         # reach it locally
kubectl rollout status deploy/order-service -n shop
kubectl rollout history deploy/order-service -n shop
kubectl rollout undo deploy/order-service -n shop
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=order-service -n shop # which pods actually receive traffic

Pod states and their usual causes

State / reason Meaning Usual causes Look at
Pending not scheduled yet insufficient CPU/memory on nodes, node selectors/taints, unbound PVC describe pod events (FailedScheduling)
ContainerCreating (stuck) pulling image / mounting volumes slow pulls, missing Secret/ConfigMap, volume attach issues events
ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull can't pull the image wrong tag, private registry without imagePullSecrets, rate limits events
CrashLoopBackOff container keeps exiting app fails at startup (bad config, missing env, can't reach DB), liveness killing a slow starter logs --previous, exit code
OOMKilled (exit 137) exceeded memory limit heap + non-heap > limit Production Debugging → OOMKilled
Exit code 143 SIGTERM normal shutdown (or killed during rollout) —
Running but 0/1 READY readiness failing dependency in readiness group down, slow warm-up, wrong probe path/port describe pod probe events, /actuator/health
Evicted removed by the kubelet node memory/disk pressure, ephemeral-storage limit describe pod, node conditions
Terminating (stuck) not finishing shutdown finalizers, app ignoring SIGTERM, long grace period describe, finalizers

Debug order for "the service isn't reachable": pods Ready? → Service selector matches pod labels (kubectl get endpointslices)? → targetPort matches the container port? → NetworkPolicy allows it? → Ingress/Gateway route and TLS correct? → DNS resolves from a test pod (kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup order-service)?

qa.q: How would you write a Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app?
qa.a: Multi-stage: build the jar in a JDK stage with dependency caching, extract Spring Boot's layers (dependencies, loader, snapshot dependencies, application) in a second stage, and copy them in that order onto a JRE (or distroless) base so code changes only rebuild the small application layer. Run as a non-root user, set heap via MaxRAMPercentage, log to stdout, tag immutably, and scan the image. Buildpacks or Jib achieve the same without a Dockerfile.

qa.q: How does the JVM size its heap in a container?
qa.a: Container-aware JVMs read the cgroup memory limit and, by default, use 25% of it for the max heap. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (typically 60–75%) instead of a fixed -Xmx so the heap follows the limit, leaving room for metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers and native memory. With small limits or under 2 CPUs the JVM also defaults to Serial GC, so choose G1 or ZGC explicitly.

qa.q: Liveness vs readiness vs startup probes?
qa.a: Startup protects slow-starting apps from being killed before they're up. Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. Liveness decides whether the container should be restarted; it should check only the process itself, never shared dependencies, or a dependency blip restarts every pod at once.

qa.q: Why do some requests fail with 502 during every rolling deploy, and how do you fix it?
qa.a: Endpoint removal is asynchronous, so a pod can receive SIGTERM and stop accepting connections while load balancers still route to it, and in-flight requests may be cut. Fix with a preStop sleep (5–15 s) so routing updates before shutdown, Spring Boot graceful shutdown to finish in-flight requests, a terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than both, readiness flipping to refusing traffic on shutdown, and maxUnavailable 0 with a PodDisruptionBudget.

qa.q: Requests vs limits — how do you set them for a Java service?
qa.a: Requests drive scheduling; limits are enforced at runtime (CPU throttling, memory OOMKill). Set memory request equal to the limit, sized from measured usage with headroom, and derive the heap from it with MaxRAMPercentage. Set CPU requests from steady-state usage; avoid tight CPU limits because they throttle JIT, GC and startup bursts, or keep the limit well above the request. Monitor throttling and right-size with VPA recommendations.

Guaranteed (every container has requests equal to limits for CPU and memory), Burstable (some requests or limits set) and BestEffort (none set). Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable ones exceeding their requests, and Guaranteed last.

qa.q: How would you autoscale a Kafka consumer service?
qa.a: On consumer lag rather than CPU, using KEDA's Kafka scaler with a target lag per replica, a minimum replica count, and a maximum no higher than the topic's partition count (extra consumers sit idle). Make processing idempotent because scaling triggers rebalances, and use cooperative rebalancing or static membership to reduce their impact.

qa.q: How do you roll out a ConfigMap change safely?
qa.a: Treat config like code: change it through git, and add a checksum of the ConfigMap to the pod template's annotations so a change triggers a normal rolling update with health checks and a one-command rollback. Validate config at startup so a bad value fails the rollout. Avoid editing live ConfigMaps that pods read in place without validation.

qa.q: What's the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet?
qa.a: A Deployment manages interchangeable stateless pods with random names and shared or no storage, ideal for web services. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable identity (ordinal name and DNS), its own persistent volume, and ordered startup and shutdown, which stateful systems like Kafka, ZooKeeper or databases need.

qa.q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. How do you debug it?
qa.a: Check kubectl logs --previous for the error from the last run and kubectl describe pod for the exit code and events. Common causes: missing or wrong config and secrets, failing to reach a dependency at startup, a liveness probe killing a slow-starting app (add a startupProbe), OOMKilled at startup, or a wrong entrypoint. Reproduce with the same image and env locally if needed.

Blue/green runs a full copy of the new version and switches all traffic at once, giving instant rollback at the cost of double capacity. Canary shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version and increases it while metrics stay healthy, limiting the blast radius of a bad release and enabling automated analysis, at the cost of needing traffic splitting and running mixed versions.

qa.q: What would you alert on for a microservice?
qa.a: Symptoms that users feel, expressed as SLOs: error rate and latency (p99) per critical endpoint, alerting on error-budget burn rate over two windows so brief blips don't page. Supplement with saturation signals that predict outages (connection pool pending, consumer lag, disk usage, certificate expiry) as lower-urgency alerts. Every page needs a runbook link and a dashboard.

cheat.devops-cheatsheet:
Building lean, secure Docker images for Spring Boot

  • Multi-stage builds with Spring Boot layers make rebuilds and pushes small.
  • Run as non-root on a JRE or distroless base; log to stdout.
  • Buildpacks and Jib build good images without a Dockerfile.
  • Tag immutably, deploy by digest, scan and sign images.

Running the JVM inside containers

  • The JVM reads cgroup limits; default max heap is only 25% of the limit — set MaxRAMPercentage.
  • CPU count comes from CPU limits; without limits, pin ActiveProcessorCount.
  • Small containers default to Serial GC: choose G1 or ZGC explicitly.
  • Speed startup with CDS/AOT caches, CRaC or native images.

Kubernetes objects every Java service uses

  • Deployments manage stateless pods through ReplicaSets; Services give stable names and load balancing.
  • ConfigMaps and Secrets inject config; PDBs protect availability during drains.
  • Spread replicas across zones; run non-root with read-only filesystems.
  • StatefulSets are for stateful systems that need identity and volumes.

Health probes and graceful shutdown

  • Startup for slow starts, readiness for traffic, liveness for restarts.
  • Never put shared dependencies in liveness checks.
  • A preStop sleep plus graceful shutdown prevents 502s during rollouts.
  • Fit shutdown phases inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

Requests, limits, QoS and autoscaling

  • Requests schedule, limits enforce: CPU over limit throttles, memory over limit kills.
  • Set memory request = limit; be cautious with CPU limits for JVMs.
  • HPA uses utilization relative to requests; scale I/O-bound services on traffic or lag (KEDA).
  • Use VPA recommendations to right-size.

Configuration and secrets on Kubernetes

  • Env vars need restarts; mounted files update in place.
  • Trigger rolling updates on config change with a checksum annotation.
  • Kubernetes Secrets are only base64: encrypt etcd, restrict RBAC, sync from a secrets manager.
  • Validate config at startup.

Rollouts, Helm and GitOps

  • Rolling updates are the default; blue/green and canaries reduce risk at a cost.
  • Argo Rollouts automates canary analysis on metrics.
  • Helm packages manifests with values; --atomic rolls back failed upgrades.
  • GitOps makes deploys pull requests and rollbacks reverts.

A CI/CD pipeline for a Java microservice

  • Stages: build/test → Testcontainers → static and dependency scans → image build/scan/sign → staging → canary.
  • Build once and promote the same image digest.
  • Keep pipelines fast with caching and parallel tests.
  • Rollback is one rehearsed command; migrations stay backward compatible.

Observability on Kubernetes: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, OpenTelemetry

  • Prometheus scrapes metrics, Loki stores logs, Tempo stores traces; Grafana ties them together.
  • Enable percentile histograms for accurate p99 across pods.
  • Alert on SLO error-budget burn rates over two windows.
  • Put trace ids in logs and use exemplars to jump from metrics to traces.

kubectl debugging cheat sheet and pod states

  • Start with get, describe, logs --previous and events.
  • Know the pod states: Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, Evicted.
  • Debug distroless pods with ephemeral containers (kubectl debug).
  • Unreachable service: readiness → selector/endpoints → ports → NetworkPolicy → ingress → DNS.
